lead: Oxy-acetylene welding burns a controlled gas flame to melt the joint edges and a filler rod. The flame is hot, about 3200 °C at its inner cone, cheap to set up and easy to control on thin sheet, repair work and site jobs where electricity is not reliable. The same station also cuts steel with an oxygen jet. The key idea is small: the oxygen-to-acetylene ratio at the torch sets the flame type, and the flame type must match the metal.
prereq: You need Chapter 4.1 for where gas welding sits among fusion processes.

blocks.text: An oxygen cylinder stands at about 150 bar; a common water capacity (internal volume) is 40 L. One bar is roughly atmospheric pressure. An acetylene cylinder stands at about 15 bar, but it is packed with a porous mass soaked in acetone. Acetylene dissolves in the acetone, so more gas can be stored safely. Each regulator reduces storage pressure to a steady working pressure. Acetylene working pressure stays near 1 bar, because free acetylene above roughly 1.5 bar can decompose without air. Hoses carry the gases to the torch. Flashback arrestors stop a flame from travelling back into a cylinder. Inside the torch, a mixing chamber sets the oxygen-to-acetylene ratio. Interchangeable tips match flame size and gas flow to plate thickness.

items: Open the cylinder valves. Set the acetylene regulator to about 1 bar and the oxygen regulator to the tip maker's pressure.
Purge each hose to remove air.
Open the torch acetylene valve a little, light the gas, then open the torch oxygen valve slowly to set the flame.
Adjust the flame to neutral, oxidising or carburising before welding.
Never use oil or grease on oxygen fittings; oxygen makes grease burn violently.

sections.h3: Flame chemistry and the three flames

blocks.text: The flame burns in two stages. In the inner cone, one volume of acetylene reacts with one volume of oxygen to give carbon monoxide and hydrogen. In the outer envelope, those gases burn with more oxygen, mostly from the surrounding air, giving carbon dioxide and water. Complete combustion needs 2.5 volumes of oxygen per volume of acetylene. The torch is not set to 2.5:1 because the outer envelope draws oxygen from air. A neutral torch setting is about 1:1 by volume. The hottest point is at the tip of the inner cone, about 3200 °C.

blocks.where: C₂H₂ is acetylene, O₂ is oxygen, CO is carbon monoxide and H₂ is hydrogen; this is the primary reaction in the inner cone.

blocks.text: Too much oxygen gives an oxidising flame: short pointed cone, hissing sound. Too much acetylene gives a carburising flame with a feather of unburned acetylene between cones. The setting is made at the torch.

blocks.text: Leftward welding moves the torch from right to left, with the filler rod ahead of the flame. It suits thin plates, usually up to about 5 mm. Rightward welding moves from left to right, with the filler rod behind the flame. It gives better penetration on thicker plates. The names describe the direction of travel, not the hand that holds the torch.
Gas cutting cuts mild steel by burning it in a jet of pure oxygen; the flame only preheats the steel.

items: Preheat the steel to its ignition temperature with a neutral flame.
Open the cutting oxygen jet. The iron burns in the oxygen, not simply melts.
Blow the iron oxide slag out of the kerf with the same jet.
Move the torch steadily along the marked line.

blocks.text: The cut width is the kerf. Drag is the lag of the bottom of the cut behind the top; too much drag means the torch is moving too fast or the oxygen pressure is wrong. Gas cutting works well on mild steel. Oxy-hydrogen gives a lower flame temperature and is used for thin work and some brazing. Air-acetylene is cheaper but cooler, common for soldering and small heating jobs.

examples.question: An oxygen cylinder has a water capacity of 40 L and is charged to 150 bar. Treat oxygen as ideal at constant temperature. (a) Find the free oxygen volume at 1 bar in litres and cubic metres. (b) A neutral flame uses oxygen and acetylene at about 1:1 by volume at the torch. An acetylene cylinder has 40 L water capacity and delivers about 6 m³ of free acetylene. How many acetylene cylinders can one oxygen cylinder serve? (c) If the torch consumes about 300 L/h of oxygen at this 1:1 setting, how long does the oxygen cylinder last?
steps: At constant temperature, p₁V₁ = p₂V₂. Here p₁ = 150 bar, V₁ = 40 L and p₂ = 1 bar.
V₂ = 150 × 40 ÷ 1 = 6000 L. Since 1000 L = 1 m³, this is 6 m³.
For acetylene, use the manufacturer's gas content: about 6 m³ (6000 L) of free acetylene per 40 L cylinder. It is stored dissolved in acetone, not as free gas at 15 bar.
Number of acetylene cylinders = 6 m³ ÷ 6 m³ = 1.
At a 1:1 torch setting the oxygen flow is also about 300 L/h. Time = 6000 L ÷ 300 L/h = 20 h.
examples.answer: Free oxygen is 6000 L (6 m³); one oxygen cylinder serves about one acetylene cylinder; the pair lasts about 20 h at 300 L/h.

traps: Neutral flame is about 1:1 by volume at the torch, not by mass. Complete combustion still needs 2.5 volumes of oxygen per volume of acetylene, with the rest drawn from air.
Acetylene cylinder pressure is about 15 bar, but the working pressure at the torch is only about 1 bar. Free acetylene above roughly 1.5 bar can decompose.
The hottest point is at the tip of the inner cone, not in the outer envelope.
Gas cutting is burning of iron in an oxygen jet, not melting by the preheat flame. The preheat only starts the reaction.
Leftward and rightward name the direction of travel; kerf is cut width and drag is the bottom lagging behind the top.

quiz.q: What is packed inside an acetylene cylinder, and why?
quiz.a: A porous mass soaked in acetone; acetylene dissolves in acetone so it can be stored safely at about 15 bar.

quiz.q: Why is acetylene working pressure kept near 1 bar?
quiz.a: Above roughly 1.5 bar, free acetylene can decompose without air. Low working pressure avoids this hazard.

quiz.q: Why is a neutral flame about 1:1 at the torch when complete combustion needs 2.5 volumes of oxygen per volume of acetylene?
quiz.a: The inner cone uses the 1:1 torch supply; the outer envelope draws the extra oxygen from surrounding air.

quiz.q: A 50 L oxygen cylinder is at 150 bar. Find free oxygen at 1 bar in litres and hours at an oxygen flow of 250 L/h.
A welder joins brass and sees white zinc fume. Which flame should be used and why?
quiz.a: A slightly oxidising flame; the oxide layer limits zinc loss. A neutral flame may overheat the brass and vaporise more zinc.

beyond: Not for the exam. Oxy-fuel stations still cut thick scrap and repair pipelines where electricity is risky. Modern shops often replace gas cutting with plasma or laser, but gas remains common on site. Cylinder design research focuses on porous mass and acetone substitutes for safer acetylene storage. Search next for oxy-fuel cutting kerf and drag, flashback arrestor standards, and alternative fuel gases such as propane and propylene.
